messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Caleb Whitmore is a 19-year-old single man of mixed North American heritage who works the afternoon shift at a fast food restaurant in the mid-sized midwestern town where he has lived his entire life. He came to the clinic on the quiet recommendation of a coworker who had noticed he seemed, in her words, "not like himself anymore." Caleb sat through the intake with his hands pressed flat against his thighs, speaking carefully, as though each sentence had been drafted somewhere before it left his mouth.

Approximately eight months ago, a severe tornado tore through the southern edge of Caleb's neighborhood on a late spring afternoon. He had been at home alone when the sirens sounded. He made it to the interior bathroom and crouched in the tub, but the storm was on him before he could do anything more — the windows blew in, a section of the ceiling came down in the hallway, and for what he estimates was three or four minutes he lay covered by debris in near-total darkness, unable to move, certain he was going to die. What he recalls most vividly is a specific smell: wet insulation, split wood, and something chemical and sharp that he has never been able to name. He remembers the sound as less important than the smell and the images — the wall cracking in a diagonal line, a piece of drywall suspended momentarily before it fell, the strange gray-green color of the light through the one remaining pane of glass. He emerged physically uninjured, but the neighborhood around him was unrecognizable, and he stood in the wreckage of his street for a long time before anyone came.

In the weeks that followed, Caleb found that simply trying to remember what had happened brought the terror back with a completeness that shocked him — not a memory of fear, but fear itself, immediate and physical. The smell became a particular problem. At the restaurant where he works the fryer vent occasionally releases an acrid, oily odor that drifts toward the front counter, and on more than one occasion Caleb has had to step to the back of the kitchen and stand still with his eyes open, waiting for the sensation to pass. He has not told his manager why. He began rehearsing his interactions before each shift — what he would say if a customer was difficult, what he would say if a coworker asked him something unexpected — because the idea of being caught off-guard, of not being ready, had become intolerable to him. He has also worked to keep the event out of his mind entirely, pushing any image or fragment away the moment it surfaces, though he has found this effort exhausting and only partially successful.

Over these months Caleb has pulled steadily away from things that carry any possibility of stress or discomfort. He declined an invitation to a friend's birthday gathering held outdoors. He stopped watching weather forecasts because he had come to believe that knowing a storm was possible was worse than not knowing. The friendships that had once been easy and frequent have thinned; several people have stopped reaching out. What frightens Caleb most, however, is not the triggers or the memories themselves but what he understands to be a fundamental change in who he is. He was certain, in a way he could not fully articulate but felt as a bodily fact, that the person he had been before the tornado — someone he described as easygoing, someone who laughed easily — was simply gone. He no longer recognized himself when he thought about how he used to be. He had come to believe that this misery was not a phase or a wound but a permanent alteration, that whatever the storm had done to him was done, and that the happy, unremarkable life he had been building was no longer available to him.

What finally brought him in was a moment at the register two weeks ago when the fryer vent released that smell and he found himself unable to speak to the customer in front of him for nearly a minute. He is hoping, with a tentativeness that he seemed almost ashamed of, that someone might tell him he is wrong about being permanently changed.
